_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning to find, collect, and organise information and data about economic and business topics.

toLevel2.question: A simple table has no link to organising prices collected from several different shops in any way.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Tables let an investigator line up prices side by side so patterns become easy to see.

distractors.explanation: Treating tables as unrelated to organising prices ignores their core role at this level.

toLevel2.question: A class survey has no link to collecting data about consumer preferences in any setting at any time.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A survey is a recognised tool for collecting data about consumer preferences in a class or school.

distractors.explanation: Treating a survey as unrelated ignores how it gathers preference data directly.

toLevel2.question: Sorting information from many sources into categories has no effect on how easy patterns are to spot.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Categorising sources groups similar information together and makes patterns easier to see.

distractors.explanation: Treating sorting as having no effect ignores how categories reveal patterns in data.

toLevel2.question: Information about a local business can be collected from a website, a visit, or an interview.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Websites, visits, and interviews are three common sources for collecting information about a business.

distractors.explanation: These three sources are widely used in research about local businesses at this level.

toLevel2.question: Recording data from a fieldwork visit in a structured way has no link to clearer findings later on.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Structured records make later analysis easier and more reliable than unsorted notes.

distractors.explanation: Treating structured records as unrelated to findings ignores their direct value.

toLevel2.question: A graph is one way to organise data about different types of work in a local area.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A graph displays counts or proportions in a way that supports clear comparison across categories.

distractors.explanation: Graphs are widely taught as a clear way to organise comparative data.

toLevel2.question: Collecting reliable data has no link at all to understanding any economic issue with evidence.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Reliable data is the basis of evidence-led understanding of economic issues.

distractors.explanation: Treating data as unrelated to evidence misses how data underpins economic understanding.

toLevel2.question: A class can collect price data by visiting three shops and recording the prices in a shared table.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Visiting shops and recording prices in a table is a clear method for collecting price data.

distractors.explanation: This method is a recognised approach to data collection at this level.

toLevel2.question: Organising information has no link to drawing conclusions in any economic investigation in any setting.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Organising information lines up evidence so conclusions can be drawn clearly from patterns seen.

distractors.explanation: Treating organisation as unrelated to conclusions ignores the role of clear data layout.

toLevel2.question: A survey can ask short questions about preferences and gather answers from many people quickly.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Surveys gather short answers from many people quickly, which is why they suit preference work.

distractors.explanation: Surveys are widely used to collect preference data quickly across many respondents.

toLevel2.question: Spotting patterns in data is exactly the same task as collecting data, with no real difference at all.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Collecting data gathers raw information; spotting patterns analyses what the data shows.

distractors.explanation: Treating the two as identical ignores the basic split between collection and analysis.

toLevel2.question: Investigation in economics rests on collected data being well organised so others can read it later.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Well-organised data lets others read and check the evidence behind a finding.

distractors.explanation: This is a recognised feature of strong investigation at this level.

toLevel2.question: Why is collecting reliable data important in an economic investigation?
toLevel2.correct: Reliable data lets a class understand an economic issue with evidence rather than guesses
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Reliable data lets a class understand an issue with evidence rather than with guesses.

distractors.answer: Reliable data has no link to understanding any economic issue in any setting at any time
distractors.explanation: Reliable data is closely linked to understanding economic issues with evidence.

distractors.answer: Reliable data always gives the answer at the start so no investigation is ever needed
distractors.explanation: Data informs investigation; it does not give every answer at the start.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is the best example of organising collected data?
toLevel2.correct: Putting prices from three shops into a table with one row per shop and one column per item
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A table with rows for shops and columns for items is a strong example of organising data.

distractors.answer: Leaving every price scribbled on loose pieces of paper without any sorting at any time
distractors.explanation: Loose unsorted scraps are unorganised data, not organised data.

distractors.answer: Refusing to write any price down and trusting memory to recall every price for every shop
distractors.explanation: Memory without records is unreliable; written, sorted records support analysis.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best describes a class survey?
toLevel2.correct: A short list of questions used to collect data about preferences from many students at once
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A class survey is a short list of questions that collects data about preferences from many students.

distractors.answer: A long story that has no link to any data collection in any class in any school in any year
distractors.explanation: A story is not a data collection tool; surveys are.

distractors.answer: A single conversation with one parent that has no link to any class preference at any time
distractors.explanation: A single parent conversation is not a class survey of student preferences.

toLevel2.question: Which source is most useful for collecting information about a local business?
toLevel2.correct: The business website, a visit to the shop, or an interview with the business owner
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Website, visit, or interview are three common sources for information about a local business.

distractors.answer: The colour of the wall behind the shop on a single Tuesday afternoon during the autumn months
distractors.explanation: Wall colour has no link to information about a business's activity.

distractors.answer: How many birds visit the shop roof during the spring months over a stretch of ten whole years
distractors.explanation: Birds on a roof have no link to information about a business's activity.

toLevel2.question: Why is sorting information into categories useful in an investigation?
toLevel2.correct: Sorting groups similar information together so patterns are easier to see across many sources
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Sorting groups similar information so patterns are easier to see across sources.

distractors.answer: Sorting has no link to seeing patterns in any kind of information in any setting at any time
distractors.explanation: Sorting is closely linked to seeing patterns in collected information.

distractors.answer: Sorting always gives the answer at the start so no further analysis is ever needed at any time
distractors.explanation: Sorting prepares analysis; it does not replace the analysis itself.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is the best example of structured fieldwork records?
toLevel2.correct: A labelled record sheet with one row per visit and clear columns for each piece of data
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A labelled record sheet with rows per visit and clear columns is a strong structured record.

distractors.answer: A pile of loose scraps with no labels, no rows, and no columns of any kind at any time
distractors.explanation: Loose scraps with no labels are unstructured records, not structured ones.

distractors.answer: A short story with no labels, no dates, and no link to any data collected on any visit
distractors.explanation: A story without labels or dates is not a structured record of fieldwork.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is the best way to display data about types of work in a local area?
toLevel2.correct: A simple bar graph that shows the count of workers in each type of work in the area
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A simple bar graph showing counts per type of work is a strong way to display the data.

distractors.answer: A blank page with no labels or numbers and no link to any type of work
distractors.explanation: A blank page does not display any data.

distractors.answer: A scoreboard from a sports match that has no link to any type of work in any local area
distractors.explanation: A sports scoreboard has no link to types of work in a local area.

toLevel2.question: Why might a class use a survey to learn about consumer preferences?
toLevel2.correct: Surveys gather short answers from many students quickly and reveal preferences across the group
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Surveys gather short answers from many students quickly and reveal preferences across the group.

distractors.answer: Surveys have no link to gathering preferences from any group of students in any class in any school
distractors.explanation: Surveys are directly linked to gathering preferences across a group.

distractors.answer: Surveys always give the same answer for every student so the result is identical for all of them
distractors.explanation: Different students give different answers, so survey results are not identical for all.

toLevel2.question: Which list includes only useful steps in collecting and organising economic data?
toLevel2.correct: Plan questions, gather data from real sources, organise data in a table, and check the records
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Planning, gathering, organising, and checking are all useful steps in collecting and organising data.

distractors.answer: Ignore the question, gather no data, leave records on loose paper, and never check anything
distractors.explanation: Ignoring the question and skipping records are the opposite of strong data work.

distractors.answer: Refuse to plan, refuse to gather data, refuse to use any table, and refuse to check any source
distractors.explanation: Refusing every step blocks rather than supports data work.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is the best example of using more than one source in research?
toLevel2.correct: Reading a website, visiting a shop, and interviewing the shop owner about the same business
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Using a website, a visit, and an interview together is strong multi-source research.

distractors.answer: Reading the same website three times in a row without using any other source at any time
distractors.explanation: Reading the same source three times is single-source, not multi-source research.

distractors.answer: Refusing to read any website and refusing to visit any shop and refusing to talk to anyone
distractors.explanation: Refusing every source is the opposite of multi-source research.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is the best example of organised data ready for analysis?
toLevel2.correct: A clear table with labelled rows and columns showing prices across three different shops
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A clear labelled table with rows and columns is organised data ready for analysis.

distractors.answer: A long sentence about prices with no labels, no rows, and no columns of any kind
distractors.explanation: A long sentence without labels is not organised data.

distractors.answer: A single number on a scrap of paper with no link to any shop or item or price
distractors.explanation: A single unlinked number does not show prices across shops.

toLevel2.question: Why is recording data in a structured way more useful than recording it on loose scraps?
toLevel2.correct: Structured records line data up clearly so later analysis is faster and more reliable
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Structured records line data up clearly, so later analysis is faster and more reliable.

distractors.answer: Structured records have no link to faster analysis or to more reliable data in any setting
distractors.explanation: Structured records are directly linked to faster, more reliable analysis.

distractors.answer: Structured records always give the answer at the start so no analysis is ever needed at any time
distractors.explanation: Structured records prepare analysis; they do not replace it.

toLevel3.question: A student gathering prices from three shops can use a table with one row per shop and one column per item.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A row-per-shop and column-per-item table is a clear, recognised way to organise price data.

distractors.explanation: This table layout is widely taught as a clear way to organise multi-shop price data.

toLevel3.question: A class survey on snack preferences will give exactly the same result whether it asks five people or fifty people.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Larger samples usually give more reliable results than very small samples in any survey.

distractors.explanation: Treating five and fifty as the same ignores how sample size affects reliability.

toLevel3.question: A graph showing different types of work in a local area can reveal which kinds of work are most common.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Graphs that compare counts across categories show which kinds of work are most common.

distractors.explanation: This is a recognised use of comparison graphs in economic study at this level.

toLevel3.question: Collecting data without organising it has no link to slower or harder analysis later in any setting at all.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Unorganised data slows analysis and makes patterns harder to spot than organised data.

distractors.explanation: Treating unorganised data as no slower ignores how layout shapes analysis time.

toLevel3.question: Sorting information from multiple sources into clear categories supports easier comparison between similar items.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Sorting into categories supports easier comparison between similar items across many sources.

distractors.explanation: Categorising is a recognised step in handling information from multiple sources.

toLevel3.question: A fieldwork visit always produces useful information whether or not the data are recorded in a structured way.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Unstructured fieldwork records often miss key details and produce less useful information later.

distractors.explanation: Treating structured and unstructured records as equally useful ignores how layout shapes recall.

toLevel3.question: An interview with a local business owner has no link to collecting any information beyond a website at all.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Interviews can gather first-hand information that does not appear on a public website.

distractors.explanation: Treating interviews as unrelated to extra information ignores their value as a first-hand source.

toLevel3.question: Reliable data has no role in any economic investigation that any class might run at any time at any school.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Reliable data is at the heart of every economic investigation in school and beyond.

distractors.explanation: Treating reliable data as having no role ignores its place at the heart of investigation.

toLevel3.question: Mia is collecting prices for three drinks at three shops. Which method best organises her data?
toLevel3.correct: A table with one row per shop and one column per drink, with each price written in its cell
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A row-per-shop, column-per-drink table is a strong way to organise multi-shop price data.

distractors.answer: A pile of loose scraps with each price written without any label or any sorting at any time
distractors.explanation: Loose unsorted scraps make data hard to read and analyse.

distractors.answer: A single sentence that lists every price in random order without any link to any shop
distractors.explanation: A single random-order sentence is not an organised data layout.

toLevel3.question: Jarrah wants to learn about a local bakery. Which combination of sources best supports his research?
toLevel3.correct: The bakery website, a visit to the bakery, and an interview with the baker about the work
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Website, visit, and interview together are a strong multi-source research approach.

distractors.answer: The colour of the bakery wall, the number of clouds above it, and the breeze in the morning
distractors.explanation: Wall colour, clouds, and breeze are not sources about a bakery's work.

distractors.answer: A scoreboard from last weekend, a song chart from last year, and a recipe book from a friend
distractors.explanation: Sports, songs, and a friend's recipe book are not sources about this bakery.

toLevel3.question: Anika runs a class survey on snack preferences. Which approach best supports a reliable result?
toLevel3.correct: Ask short, clear questions to as many students as possible, then organise the answers in a table
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Short, clear questions to many students with results in a table support a reliable survey.

distractors.answer: Ask long, vague questions to two students once, then trust the answers as the whole class view
distractors.explanation: Two students with long vague questions does not represent the whole class reliably.

distractors.answer: Ask no questions and refuse to record any answer from any student at any time of any year
distractors.explanation: Asking no questions and recording no answers is the opposite of survey work.

toLevel3.question: Sam wants to organise data about types of work in his local area. Which display fits the goal best?
toLevel3.correct: A simple bar graph showing the count of workers in each type of work in his local area
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A bar graph of counts per type of work fits the goal of organising the data clearly.

distractors.answer: A blank page with no labels or numbers and no link to any type of work in any local area
distractors.explanation: A blank page does not display any data.

distractors.answer: A scoreboard from last weekend's game with no link to any type of work in any local area
distractors.explanation: A sports scoreboard has no link to types of work in a local area.

toLevel3.question: Lila gathers fieldwork notes during a visit to a local shop. Which approach best produces useful records?
toLevel3.correct: Use a labelled record sheet with one row per observation and clear columns for each kind of detail
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A labelled record sheet with rows per observation and clear columns produces useful records.

distractors.answer: Write whatever comes to mind on loose scraps with no labels, no rows, and no columns of any kind
distractors.explanation: Loose scraps without labels are unstructured records, not useful ones.

distractors.answer: Write nothing during the visit and trust memory to recall every detail at any later time
distractors.explanation: Writing nothing leaves no record; memory alone is unreliable.

toLevel3.question: Kofi is sorting research notes from a website, an interview, and a survey. Which method best fits the task?
toLevel3.correct: Sort the notes into clear categories that match the questions the investigation set out to answer
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Sorting notes into categories that match the investigation questions fits the task best.

distractors.answer: Sort the notes by the colour of the paper they are written on with no other link
distractors.explanation: Paper colour has no link to the content or to the investigation questions.

distractors.answer: Refuse to sort the notes and leave them mixed with no link to any topic
distractors.explanation: Refusing to sort leaves the notes hard to use in any analysis.

toLevel3.question: Yen wants to compare prices of three school items across two shops. Which layout best supports the comparison?
toLevel3.correct: A table with one row per item and one column per shop, with each price in its own cell
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A row-per-item, column-per-shop table supports clear comparison across the two shops.

distractors.answer: A long paragraph that lists every price in random order with no link to any shop or any item
distractors.explanation: A random-order paragraph makes comparison harder, not easier.

distractors.answer: A blank page with no rows, no columns, and no prices written down for any of the items
distractors.explanation: A blank page does not record any data and supports no comparison.

toLevel3.question: Rosa is collecting opinions about a new playground equipment plan. Which method gathers the most data quickly?
toLevel3.correct: A short class survey that asks two or three clear questions and records the answers in a table
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A short class survey with clear questions and a table gathers many opinions quickly.

distractors.answer: A series of long one-on-one conversations with no record kept and no clear question
distractors.explanation: Long conversations with no records gather slowly and lose information.

distractors.answer: A refusal to ask any opinion and a plan to use no data when discussing the playground
distractors.explanation: Refusing to ask collects no data at all.

toLevel3.question: Amir wants to record results from a fieldwork visit to a market. Which approach best produces a usable record?
toLevel3.correct: Use a structured record sheet with one row per stall and clear columns for prices and goods
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A structured record sheet with rows per stall and clear columns produces a usable market record.

distractors.answer: Write a single short sentence with no labels and no link to any stall or any price at any time
distractors.explanation: A single unlabelled sentence is not a usable record of market data.

distractors.answer: Write nothing during the visit and trust memory to fill in every detail at any later time at home
distractors.explanation: Writing nothing leaves no record; memory alone is unreliable for fieldwork details.

toLevel3.question: Jade has notes from three sources about a local business. Which step makes the notes easiest to use later?
toLevel3.correct: Sort the notes into categories that match each part of the question being investigated
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Sorting notes by category makes them easiest to use in later analysis.

distractors.answer: Mix every note into a single pile with no link to any source or to any part of the question
distractors.explanation: Mixing notes makes them harder, not easier, to use later.

distractors.answer: Throw out every note immediately and rely on memory of each source for every later analysis step
distractors.explanation: Throwing out notes leaves no records to support later analysis.

toLevel3.question: Linh wants to investigate which type of work is most common in her area. Which data display fits the goal?
toLevel3.correct: A simple bar graph showing the count of workers in each type of work in her local area
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A simple bar graph of counts per type of work fits the goal of finding the most common type.

distractors.answer: A scoreboard from last weekend's match with no link to any type of work in any local area
distractors.explanation: A sports scoreboard has no link to types of work in a local area.

distractors.answer: A blank page with no labels or numbers and no link to any type of work
distractors.explanation: A blank page does not display any data.

toLevel3.question: Marcus collects survey answers from twenty classmates about lunch choices. Which step best organises the data?

toLevel3.correctExplanation: Tallying answers in a table and turning the totals into a bar graph organises survey data well.

distractors.answer: Refuse to count any answer and leave the survey results in a pile of unsorted loose scraps
distractors.explanation: Refusing to count leaves the survey data unorganised and hard to use.

distractors.explanation: Throwing out notes leaves no record to support later analysis.

toLevel5.question: A student claims that 'unorganised data is just as easy to analyse as organised data'. Which response best evaluates this claim?
toLevel5.correct: The claim is misleading because organised data lets investigators see patterns more quickly and clearly
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Organised data lets investigators see patterns more quickly and clearly than unorganised data.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct because every set of data is always equally easy to analyse in every situation
distractors.explanation: Data layout strongly affects analysis time and clarity.

distractors.answer: The claim is correct because no investigation ever needs data to be organised in any setting
distractors.explanation: Investigations regularly rely on organised data; treating it as unneeded is wrong.

toLevel5.question: Two friends debate whether a small survey can represent a whole school. Which evaluation best fits the topic?

distractors.explanation: Whether a parent is present has no link to how representative a survey is.

distractors.explanation: Investigations regularly use fieldwork records; treating them as unused is wrong.

distractors.explanation: Investigations almost always benefit from more than one source of information.
